To distract someone means to pull their attention away from what they are focused on, and redirect it toward something else.

Think of attention like a spotlight. Whatever you're focused on is in that spotlight. When something distracts you, it snatches that spotlight away — even if just for a moment — and points it somewhere else.
Who or What Can Distract?

Both people and things can distract.

  • A person can distract another person.
    • She distracted the guard while her friend slipped past.
  • A thing (noise, smell, thought, movement) can distract a person.
    • The loud music distracted him while he was studying.
    • A sudden movement distracted the cat.

You can also distract yourself — intentionally or not.

  • He distracted himself with video games to avoid thinking about his problems.
The Grammar Pattern

The most natural way to use this verb:

distract + someone + from + something

  • Don't distract me from my work.
  • The pain distracted her from enjoying the trip.
  • His jokes distracted the children from their fear.

You will also see it without "from" when the context is already clear:

  • Stop distracting me!
  • The noise is distracting everyone.
Intentional vs. Unintentional

This is an important distinction. Distracting can be done on purpose or it can happen accidentally.

Intentional — someone deliberately pulls attention away:

  • The magician's assistant distracted the audience with a wave of her hand so the magician could switch the cards.
  • The soldiers created a loud disturbance to distract the enemy from the real attack.

Unintentional — something just happens to pull attention away, with no deliberate effort:

  • The ticking clock distracted me during the exam. (The clock didn't try to — it just did.)
  • Her perfume distracted him so much that he forgot what he was saying.

Both uses are completely correct and common. Context usually makes it clear which kind is meant.
Positive and Negative Uses

People often think of distraction as a bad thing — and it frequently is. But the word itself is neutral. It simply describes attention being shifted. Whether that is good or bad depends on the situation.

Negative — attention is pulled away from something important:

  • Texting while driving is dangerous because it distracts the driver.
  • Her worries distracted her from concentrating on the interview.

Positive — attention is pulled away from something painful or difficult:

  • The nurse distracted the child with a toy while giving the injection.
  • He used work to distract himself from his grief.
  • Playing music distracted her from the long, boring wait.

In the positive sense, distracting someone (or yourself) is actually a kind or helpful act — you are giving someone's mind a break from something painful.
Degree and Intensity

Distraction is not always total. You can be slightly distracted or completely distracted.

  • The background noise slightly distracted her, but she managed to finish.
  • He was so distracted by his phone that he walked into a pole.

The verb itself does not carry intensity built in, so speakers use adverbs like slightly, badly, completely, easily, constantly to show how strong the effect is.
The Idea of "Drawing Away"

A subtle but important point: to distract is not just to stop someone from focusing — it is to actively draw their attention toward something else. There is a pull involved, not just a block.

Compare:

  • If a website crashes and you can't work, your work is stopped — but nothing distracted you.
  • If a notification pops up and your eyes jump to it, your attention has been distracted — pulled away and pointed elsewhere.

The difference is that distraction involves a competing thing that wins (at least briefly) over what you were focused on.
Common Collocations (Words That Often Pair With "Distract")

These are phrases you will see and hear often:

  • easily distracted — someone who loses focus readily
    • Young children are easily distracted.
  • distract attention from — redirect notice away from something
    • The scandal distracted public attention from the real issues.
  • distract oneself — intentionally shift your own focus
    • She distracted herself by going for a walk.
  • distract with — pull attention using something specific
    • He distracted her with a funny story.
The Related Forms You Will Encounter

Since you want to recognize this word in all its forms:

Distracting (adjective/present participle) — something that causes distraction; describes the thing that pulls attention.

  • That music is very distracting.
  • He found her laugh distracting.

Distracted (adjective/past participle) — describes the person whose attention has been pulled away; the state of not being fully focused.

  • She seemed distracted during the meeting.
  • A distracted driver is a dangerous driver.
  • He answered in a distracted way, barely listening.

Distraction (noun) — the act of distracting, or the thing that causes it.

  • The phone is a constant distraction.
  • He needed a distraction from his stress.
  • She finished the puzzle without any distraction.
Summary in One Sentence

To distract is to pull someone's attention away from what they are currently focused on — whether deliberately or by accident, and whether that turns out to be helpful or harmful.

Once you understand that core pull — attention being drawn away — every use of this word, in every context, will make immediate sense.
